title: Part 5 · Reading multiple choice
subtitle: Reading and Use of English · 6 questions
instructions: Questions 31–36. Choose A, B, C or D. Two marks per answer.
passage:
When the rehearsal room went quiet
On the first evening of a community music project, I arrived carrying a notebook and a confident plan. I had been asked to make an audio portrait of the group for a local exhibition. As a radio producer, I knew how to gather a lively introduction: ask people why they had joined, record a little music, then find a memorable closing remark. I expected the hardest problem to be background noise. Instead, when I placed the recorder on the table, conversation stopped. Several people looked at it as if it were an additional participant whose intentions nobody understood.
The conductor suggested beginning with the rehearsal and leaving interviews until later. I agreed, although privately I worried that the most interesting spontaneous comments would be lost. For the next hour I sat against the wall. A melody that initially sounded confused gradually became recognisable as players listened and adjusted to one another. I noticed that a joke, a short demonstration and a patient repetition often achieved more than a long explanation. My original plan had assumed that the meaning of the project would be found mainly in what people said about it. Now I wondered whether it was also present in how they worked together.
At the break, a violinist named Rosa asked whether she could listen to a small part of the recording. I expected her to comment on the quality of the playing. Instead, she pointed out that her chair made a loud noise whenever she moved. She was worried that listeners would think she was interrupting deliberately. Another member asked if the final piece would include names. These were reasonable questions, yet my information sheet had not made their answers clear. I had explained the exhibition's purpose in general terms without showing what being recorded might feel like to a particular person.
We agreed on a different approach. I would return for three rehearsals, and at each one members could hear selected material and discuss how it might be used. Anyone could ask for a contribution to be left out. This did not give every participant control over every editing decision, but it created a way to raise concerns before the exhibition opened. It also meant more work than the single visit I had budgeted for. I reduced another part of the production rather than pretending that meaningful consultation could happen without time.
During the second visit, people largely ignored the recorder. That was useful, but I no longer treated their lack of attention as proof that I had solved every ethical question. A familiar object can still capture something unexpected. When one player described a difficult personal experience, I asked separately whether she wanted it included. She decided against it. The story might have made a dramatic moment in the final piece, but drama was not the only measure of a good edit. The finished portrait needed to be something the group could recognise without feeling that its trust had been used against it.
The final recording included more pauses than I had anticipated. In one passage, listeners hear an uncertain beginning, the conductor's brief suggestion and a stronger second attempt. I left that sequence almost untouched because the change was audible without explanation. At the exhibition, a visitor told me the quiet moments made the group sound approachable: learning seemed possible rather than embarrassing. I could not claim that every listener responded that way. Still, the comment reminded me why the project had improved. By abandoning the assumption that I already knew where its meaning would be, I had learned to listen before deciding what the audience should hear.

title: Part 6 · Gapped text
subtitle: Reading and Use of English · 6 questions
instructions: Questions 37–42. Choose a sentence A–G for each gap. Use each chosen sentence once. Two marks per answer.
passage:
A history made together
Our neighbourhood association began collecting old photographs for a small display. We imagined a simple job: ask residents for pictures, write captions and arrange them in date order. The first donation was a photograph of a crowded street. On the back, someone had written the name of a shop, but the building in the picture now housed a dentist. We realised that the same place could connect several periods and several kinds of experience. [37]
Soon, residents were bringing memories as well as photographs. One remembered waiting outside the shop as a child, while another had delivered goods to its rear entrance. They disagreed about the colour of the sign, but each described a different decade. [38] We began recording when each person had known a place and which details they were certain about. Disagreement was something to investigate rather than erase.
Dating the photographs was another challenge. A car model or a cinema poster sometimes offered a clue, but one image showed neither. The donor remembered finding it among a relative's possessions and could say nothing about when it was taken. [39] The caption explained what was known and invited further information. This felt more honest than a precise-looking answer with no evidence behind it.
As the collection grew, people wanted to see how familiar locations related to one another. A school photograph and a factory picture seemed unrelated until a visitor explained that many pupils' parents had worked at the factory. [40] Threads linked photographs to streets, and coloured notes distinguished direct recollections from suggestions that still needed checking. The display gradually became a record of enquiry as well as a record of places.
We noticed that some streets had many photographs while others had none. At first this looked like a failure of the collection. Then we used the gaps to ask for contributions from people who had not yet visited. [41] A resident brought a picture of a laundry behind her grandparents' home, adding a kind of working life that the collection had previously missed.
When the exhibition opened, visitors asked for copies of several photographs. Before agreeing, we checked what each donor had permitted and whether identifiable people raised additional concerns. [42] Collecting memories had created relationships, and those relationships still mattered after the display looked complete. We now keep a record of permissions beside the captions, so future volunteers can understand both the images and the conditions under which they were shared.

instructions: Questions 43–52. Choose person A–D. Each person may be chosen more than once. One mark per answer.
passage:
Four people describe learning a practical skill
A — Daniel, bicycle maintenance
I joined the class after paying for a simple repair I later realised I could have done myself. Saving money was the attraction, although it has not been the most important result. I used to feel helpless when a bicycle made an unfamiliar noise. Now I can describe what is happening and decide whether it is a job for a mechanic. The instructor insisted that we should know when to stop, which made me trust him more. I expected to watch demonstrations for most of the session, but we spent almost all the time working in pairs. My partner noticed when I skipped a step, and explaining my own method helped me understand it. I still keep a small checklist in my tool bag. Being able to do something once in class is different from remembering the order several weeks later, especially when I am in a hurry to get somewhere.

B — Elif, pottery
My first pot collapsed, and the second was so heavy that I could barely lift it. I had imagined taking home something elegant after one lesson. Fortunately, the tutor showed us one of her early attempts, which looked much like mine. That changed the atmosphere. We could laugh at mistakes without pretending they were good work. I practise at the studio because I have neither the equipment nor a suitable space at home. The journey takes an hour, so I cannot go as often as I would like. Still, the time there has become a welcome break from my office routine. I do not check messages while my hands are covered in clay. Friends keep suggesting that I should sell pieces, but making the activity into a business would remove the reason I enjoy it. I am happy to improve slowly without a customer waiting for a perfect result.

C — Rosa, repairing clothes
I inherited a sewing machine that I did not know how to use. An online video helped me thread it, but I needed a class to understand why the fabric kept pulling to one side. The tutor watched my hands and spotted the problem immediately. Since then, I have been more careful about choosing a learning method to suit the difficulty. Video is convenient for reviewing a familiar step; individual feedback is better when I cannot identify what I am doing wrong. I had worried I would be the youngest person in the room, but the range of ages made no difference once we began working. My most satisfying repair was to a coat my mother had worn for years. Its value was personal, not financial. She had been ready to stop wearing it, and I liked being able to return something familiar to use.

D — Owen, growing vegetables
I started because my neighbour offered me part of her garden. I thought the spare space was the difficult thing to obtain; in fact, making time to visit regularly was harder. At first I chose too many crops and lost track of what needed attention. The next year I reduced the variety and kept a diary of what I planted and when. This made patterns easier to notice. I also stopped comparing my small harvest with photographs posted by experienced growers. Those pictures rarely showed the unsuccessful plants. Now a few useful meals matter more to me than producing an impressive image. My neighbour and I share jobs when one of us is away, and we discuss changes before making them. The arrangement works because we are clear about responsibility, rather than because both of us always have the same amount of free time.
